concepts.name: Ideological Divide: Moderates vs Extremists — Core Differences
key_dimensions: Difference in methods: constitutional agitation (Moderates) vs mass mobilization and direct action (Extremists)
Difference in goals: administrative reforms within British framework (Moderates) vs Swaraj as complete self-rule (Extremists)
Difference in faith in British justice: Moderates believed in British goodwill; Extremists rejected it entirely
UPSC Trap: Moderates did NOT oppose Swaraj as a concept — they differed on the method and timeline to achieve it

concepts.name: Bal Gangadhar Tilak's Role and Ideological Position
key_dimensions: Tilak as the principal Extremist leader and his formula of 'Swaraj is my birthright'
His use of Ganesh Chaturthi and Shivaji festivals as tools of mass political mobilization
His opposition to the moderate leadership of Gokhale and Pherozeshah Mehta at Surat
UPSC Trap: Tilak was NOT anti-reform — he opposed gradualism and petitioning, not the goal of self-governance

concepts.name: Gopal Krishna Gokhale's Moderate Leadership and Congress Presidency
key_dimensions: Gokhale as the leading Moderate voice and mentor figure in Congress
His belief in 'political training' of Indians through gradual constitutional reform
His role in trying to preserve Congress unity before the Surat session
UPSC Trap: Gokhale was NOT personally anti-nationalist — Gandhi considered him his political guru despite ideological differences with Extremists

concepts.name: The Calcutta Congress Session 1906 — Prelude to the Split
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji's presidential address where 'Swaraj' was formally adopted as the Congress goal — a key concession to Extremists
The four resolutions passed: Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education — significant victory for Extremist agenda
The compromise on leadership (Naoroji as neutral president) that temporarily held Congress together
UPSC Trap: The 1906 session is often confused as the split session — the split actually occurred at Surat in 1907

concepts.name: The Surat Session 1907 — Sequence of Events and Immediate Causes
key_dimensions: Dispute over the election of Congress President: Extremists backed Lala Lajpat Rai; Moderates pushed for Rash Behari Ghosh
The physical disruption of the session — shoe-throwing incident and breakdown of proceedings
Moderates' adoption of a new Congress constitution that effectively excluded Extremists
UPSC Trap: The split was not purely spontaneous — it was partly engineered by Moderate old guard (Pherozeshah Mehta's faction) who wanted to expel Extremists

concepts.name: Pherozeshah Mehta's Role in Orchestrating the Split
key_dimensions: Mehta as the dominant Moderate organizer who strategically used the Surat session to sideline Extremists
His control over the Bombay Congress machinery and influence over session logistics
Contrast between Mehta's tactical hardball and Gokhale's more conciliatory approach
UPSC Trap: Students often attribute the split solely to ideological differences — Mehta's political maneuvering was equally decisive

concepts.name: The Swadeshi and Boycott Movement as the Catalytic Context
key_dimensions: Partition of Bengal 1905 as the immediate trigger that energized Extremists and exposed Moderate limitations
Debate within Congress on whether Boycott should extend beyond Bengal and beyond goods to institutions
Extremists' broader interpretation of Boycott (including government schools, courts) vs Moderates' limited economic interpretation
UPSC Trap: Swadeshi was accepted by both factions — the disagreement was over the scope and method of Boycott

concepts.name: Lala Lajpat Rai — The Extremist Candidate and Punjab Connection
key_dimensions: His nomination as Extremist candidate for Congress presidency at Surat 1907
His deportation to Mandalay in 1907 (same year) by British authorities — significance of timing
His role in Bal-Pal-Lal triumvirate and how his absence weakened Extremist coordination

UPSC Trap: Lajpat Rai's deportation in 1907 is sometimes confused as a consequence of the Surat split — it was actually a British action against Extremist activity in Punjab, occurring in the same year

concepts.name: The 'Lal-Bal-Pal' Triumvirate — Composition and Significance
key_dimensions: Lala Lajpat Rai (Punjab), Bal Gangadhar Tilak (Maharashtra), Bipin Chandra Pal (Bengal) as the three Extremist pillars
Each represented a regional mass movement: agrarian discontent, Maratha pride, Bengal's anti-partition agitation
The triumvirate's inability to maintain organizational unity after the split
UPSC Trap: Aurobindo Ghosh was equally important ideologically but is NOT part of the 'Lal-Bal-Pal' formulation — a frequent exam trap

concepts.name: Bipin Chandra Pal's Ideological Contribution to Extremism
key_dimensions: Pal as the principal theorist of 'Passive Resistance' as a political method
His journal 'New India' as a platform for Extremist ideology
His eventual break with Tilak and withdrawal from active politics post-split — a lesser-known but important development
UPSC Trap: Passive Resistance as articulated by Pal is distinct from Gandhian Non-cooperation — it predates Gandhi's entry and lacks the same mass ethical framework

concepts.name: Aurobindo Ghosh's Role — Ideologue of Extremism
key_dimensions: Aurobindo as the chief intellectual architect of Extremist philosophy in 'Yugantar' and 'Karmayogin'
His concept of 'Nationalism as a Religion' — spiritualizing political struggle
His withdrawal from politics after the Alipore Bomb Case (1908) and transition to spiritual pursuits at Pondicherry
UPSC Trap: Aurobindo is frequently misplaced as a Bengal revolutionary only — his all-India ideological influence on Extremism is broader

concepts.name: New Congress Constitution of 1907 — Moderates' Organizational Consolidation
key_dimensions: The new constitution imposed strict conditions for Congress membership, effectively designed to exclude Extremists
Requirement of allegiance to constitutional methods as a membership criterion
How this constitutional maneuver by Moderates converted an ideological rift into a formal organizational split
UPSC Trap: The split is often described as 'mutual' — in reality the Moderates used procedural and organizational means to expel Extremists, making it an asymmetric action

concepts.name: British Policy Response to the Split — Divide and Rule Dimension
key_dimensions: The Morley-Minto Reforms 1909 as the British response designed to reward Moderate cooperation and isolate Extremists
British support (tacit) for Moderate dominance as a means of containing radical nationalism
Tilak's prosecution under Sedition Law 1908 (6-year transportation to Mandalay) as direct British action against Extremists post-split
UPSC Trap: Morley-Minto Reforms (1909) are often studied in isolation — their connection to the Surat split as a calculated British political reward to Moderates is frequently missed

concepts.name: Tilak's Sedition Trial 1908 — Consequences of the Split
key_dimensions: Tilak prosecuted under Section 124A IPC for articles in 'Kesari' after the Muzaffarpur bomb case
His famous courtroom defense — 'Swaraj is my birthright' speech
His six-year imprisonment in Mandalay (1908–1914) and its effect on the Extremist movement's continuity
UPSC Trap: The 1908 trial is sometimes confused with his earlier 1897 sedition case — he faced two separate sedition trials, each with different contexts

concepts.name: Re-unification at Lucknow 1916 — Conditions and Significance
key_dimensions: Tilak's return from Mandalay and re-admission to Congress in 1916 as the basis of reunification
Lucknow Pact 1916 as the broader political context uniting Congress and Muslim League
The Annie Besant Home Rule League movement as pressure that hastened Congress reunification
UPSC Trap: The reunification is often credited solely to Tilak's political moderation — in fact it was also driven by the First World War context and Besant's organizational pressure

concepts.name: National Education Movement — Extremist Alternative Institution Building
key_dimensions: The Extremist demand for National Education as one of the four resolutions of the 1906 Calcutta session
Establishment of National Schools and Colleges in Bengal as part of Boycott of government educational institutions
Contrast with Moderate approach of working within existing British-run educational institutions
UPSC Trap: National Education is one of the FOUR demands of the Swadeshi era (Swaraj, Swadeshi, Boycott, National Education) — exams often test whether students can correctly name all four

concepts.name: The Role of Regional Press and Vernacular Journalism in Extremism
key_dimensions: Tilak's 'Kesari' (Marathi) and 'Mahratta' (English) as primary organs of Extremist ideology
Aurobindo's 'Yugantar' and Bipin Pal's 'New India' as pan-India Extremist platforms
British use of Sedition laws and Press Acts against these publications as a pattern of political suppression
UPSC Trap: 'Kesari' was in Marathi and 'Mahratta' in English — both were Tilak's newspapers; exams frequently swap the languages

concepts.name: Assessment of Moderate Achievements and Their Historical Vindication
key_dimensions: R.C. Majumdar and Bipan Chandra debate: were Moderates 'safety valves' for British rule or genuine nationalists?
Moderate contributions: establishing political consciousness, economic critique (Drain Theory by Dadabhai Naoroji), constitutional precedents
Argument that Moderate methods laid groundwork for mass politics — continuity rather than contradiction with Extremism
UPSC Trap: The question 'Were Moderates more harmful than helpful?' is a classic Mains trap — balanced analysis requires acknowledging both their limitations AND their foundational contributions

concepts.name: Drain of Wealth Theory — Moderate Economic Nationalism as Intellectual Foundation
key_dimensions: Dadabhai Naoroji's 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901) as the seminal text
The theory's argument: India's poverty was a structural result of British economic exploitation, not natural backwardness
How Drain Theory was the intellectual bridge between Moderate constitutionalism and Extremist anti-imperialism
UPSC Trap: Drain Theory is often exclusively attributed to Naoroji — R.C. Dutt's 'Economic History of India' and Gokhale's budget speeches were equally important elaborations

concepts.name: Swadeshi Movement's Social Dimensions — Beyond Economics
key_dimensions: Swadeshi's impact on women's participation in public life for the first time in significant numbers
Its role in generating indigenous entrepreneurship and early industrial nationalism (e.g., Bengal Chemical, textile mills)
The tension within Swadeshi between upper-caste Hindu symbolism and Muslim alienation — seeds of communal divergence
UPSC Trap: Swadeshi is frequently examined only as an economic boycott — its social mobilization dimensions (women, peasants, students) and its communal complications are higher-yield for Mains
